case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Heck v. Humphrey favorable-termination bar prevents a plaintiff who has an outstanding criminal conviction from pursuing a federal civil-rights suit seeking prospective declaratory and injunctive relief against a municipality’s allegedly unconstitutional enforcement practices.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (as limited by the judicially created Heck v. Humphrey doctrine); U.S. Const. amend. I (speech/assembly) and amend. XIV (due process/equal protection) as the underlying constitutional rights asserted.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Olivier argues that Heck should not be extended to block forward-looking relief (declaratory/injunctive) aimed at preventing future unconstitutional enforcement, because such relief does not function as a collateral attack on a past conviction in the way damages would. He maintains that allowing municipalities to invoke Heck to defeat prospective challenges effectively insulates allegedly unconstitutional ordinances/policies from judicial review whenever the plaintiff has been convicted, chilling First Amendment activity and leaving no meaningful avenue to prevent recurring enforcement. Petitioner-supported amici (e.g., FIRE, Manhattan Institute, ACLJ, YAF) emphasize that the Fifth Circuit’s approach overreads Heck, conflicts with the purpose of § 1983, and undermines core First Amendment protections by forcing speakers to choose between foregoing speech or risking unreviewable convictions that then bar prospective relief.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City of Brandon contends that Olivier’s requested prospective relief would necessarily imply the invalidity of his still-outstanding conviction (because it would require a federal court to declare the underlying enforcement unconstitutional), so Heck bars the suit unless and until he achieves favorable termination through direct appeal, state post-conviction remedies, or federal habeas. Respondents and their amici further argue that this case is a poor vehicle even apart from Heck: the claims may be forfeited or inadequately preserved, and other preclusion-type doctrines (forfeiture, estoppel, res judicata) could independently defeat relief on remand; they also point to related Fifth Circuit litigation (including Siders v. City of Brandon) as demonstrating procedural and factual complications that make Supreme Court review unnecessary or premature.
key_precedents: Siders v. City of Brandon, Mississippi

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest objection: that the declaration and injunction, as pleaded, would in practical operation condemn the very enforcement that produced Olivier’s still-valid conviction, creating the incompatible-judgments problem Heck aimed to avoid. But Heck already supplies an administrable, bright-line standard—whether success in the §1983 action would necessarily imply the conviction’s invalidity—and that rule is preferable to a broader, more amorphous bar on forward-looking relief whenever a conviction exists. I agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett that we must look to the practical effect of the requested relief, but the correct response is partial application and narrowing: bar or deny only those forms of declaratory or injunctive relief that would necessarily negate the outstanding judgment, while permitting genuinely prospective constraints on future enforcement to proceed if they can be awarded without an incompatible determination. That approach addresses the end-run concern without extending Heck beyond its necessity-based boundary and leaves ordinary tailoring and justiciability questions for the lower courts on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan rightly emphasize that Heck is not a categorical bar to all prospective relief and that some decrees can be tailored to avoid implying invalidity. But Justice Barrett and Justice Alito correctly focus on this suit as pleaded and in practical operation: Olivier’s requested declaration and injunction would brand unconstitutional the very enforcement that produced his still-outstanding conviction, inviting the “two conflicting resolutions” and federal–state friction that Heck was designed to prevent. That limitation accords with the 1871 common-law backdrop, which generally precluded collateral civil attacks on extant criminal judgments absent favorable termination, and Heck properly incorporates that historically grounded constraint into § 1983. If Olivier can identify genuinely forward-looking relief that regulates future conduct without condemning the predicate for his conviction, that is a different case and should be brought and litigated on that footing—not achieved by judicial narrowing that rewrites the complaint.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s necessity-focused framing correctly reflects Heck’s stated test, and I agree Heck is not a categorical bar to all prospective relief. But Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas are right to insist we decide this case as pleaded and by its practical operation: Olivier’s requested declaration and injunction would adjudicate unconstitutional the very enforcement actions that produced his still-outstanding conviction, creating the incompatible-resolutions problem Heck was designed to prevent. Labeling that as a mere tailoring issue risks allowing plaintiffs to plead their way into a federal merits judgment that functionally serves as an end-run around habeas, with the conviction still on the books. A genuinely forward-looking, policy-only injunction that can be entered without condemning the predicate of the conviction might be permissible in another case, but that is not this one.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett rightly press that, as pleaded, some of Olivier’s requested declaratory language risks a practical incompatibility with a still-valid conviction, the very concern Heck sought to prevent. But that is an argument for applying Heck with precision, not for expanding it categorically: as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Heck’s implied, purpose-limited bar is triggered only where success would necessarily imply invalidity or otherwise function as a direct challenge to custody, and genuinely prospective regulation of future enforcement can be fashioned without vacating, shortening, or undermining the conviction. Where particular declarations would cross the line, ordinary tailoring (or partial dismissal of that retrospective component) is the proper response, rather than insulating ongoing municipal practices from § 1983 review when habeas supplies no comparable prospective remedy. Extending Heck to any forward-looking relief whenever a conviction exists would overshoot Heck’s anti-“swamping” rationale and distort the § 1983/habeas boundary our cases (including Skinner and Wilkinson) have drawn.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett raise the hardest point: as pleaded, Olivier’s declaration/injunction could be read to condemn the very enforcement underlying a still-valid conviction, inviting Heck’s “two conflicting resolutions” concern. But Heck’s implicit exception is triggered only when success would necessarily imply the invalidity of the conviction or operate as a bid for immediate or speedier release; overlap in facts or rhetoric is not enough, and (as the Chief Justice emphasizes) genuinely prospective relief can be fashioned to regulate future enforcement without adjudicating the conviction’s validity. The proper response to overbroad requested language is not a categorical expansion of Heck, but a relief-by-relief application of the “necessarily implies” inquiry, with narrowing or denial only to the extent a particular declaration would function as a retrospective judgment of invalidity. That approach preserves § 1983’s breadth while respecting habeas’s distinct procedural limits, and it avoids insulating ongoing municipal practices from forward-looking review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett press the case’s hardest point: that Olivier’s requested declaration and injunction, as pleaded, may in practical operation condemn the very enforcement that produced his still-valid conviction and so risk Heck’s “two conflicting resolutions.” But Heck’s own limiting principle is narrower and more administrable—whether success in the §1983 action would “necessarily imply” the conviction’s invalidity—and, as the Chief Justice explains, prospective relief can often be tailored to regulate future enforcement without adjudicating the conviction’s lawfulness. The proper course is not to expand Heck into a categorical bar whenever a conviction exists, but to require the lower courts to apply the necessary-implication inquiry to each form of requested relief and to deny or narrow only those portions that would function as a collateral attack. If the declaratory language is overbroad here, that is a remedial tailoring and framing problem for remand, not a warrant to rewrite Heck beyond its terms and purposes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest point for Respondent: that Olivier’s requested declaration/injunction, in practical operation, could condemn the very enforcement predicate for his still-valid conviction and thus invite the inconsistent-judgments and collateral-attack concerns that animate Heck. But, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Heck’s administrable gatekeeping rule is necessity—whether success in the § 1983 action would necessarily imply the conviction’s invalidity—not mere factual overlap or the possibility that a broadly worded decree could be read to undercut a conviction. The better course is to permit genuinely prospective relief to proceed to the extent it can be awarded without an incompatible determination, while barring or narrowing any retrospective declaratory component that would function as a de facto invalidation of the outstanding judgment. Extending Heck categorically to all forward-looking relief whenever a conviction exists would overshoot the historically grounded favorable-termination limits and unduly insulate ongoing enforcement regimes from review.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s proposed line—apply Heck only to relief that would “necessarily imply” invalidity—is right as far as it goes, but it does not answer the threshold problem Justice Thomas and Justice Alito identify: we must evaluate this case as pleaded and in its practical operation under existing state law. On this record, Olivier’s requested declarations and injunctions would functionally pronounce unconstitutional the enforcement that produced his still-outstanding conviction, thereby obstructing the State’s ability to maintain and enforce that judgment—the precise habeas/§ 1983 boundary Heck polices to avoid incompatible adjudications and an end-run around habeas’s federalism-protective constraints. Justice Kagan’s suggestion that we can simply “narrow” the declaratory language depends on rewriting the claim into a different, genuinely prospective vehicle; that may be possible in another suit, but we should not decide this one on a hypothetical narrowing. The proper disposition is to affirm dismissal (or at least hold Heck bars the relief sought here as framed), leaving Olivier free to file a forward-looking complaint that can be adjudicated without condemning the predicate for his conviction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett raise the sharpest concern: that, as pleaded, Olivier’s requested declaration and injunction could operate as a condemnation of the very enforcement that produced his still-valid conviction, creating the incompatible-judgments problem Heck targets. But Heck is an implied, purpose-bound limitation on § 1983, and its trigger is the necessity inquiry—whether success would “necessarily imply” invalidity—not a categorical bar whenever a conviction exists. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, courts can and should parse forms of relief, barring or narrowing any declaration that would function as a retrospective invalidation while permitting genuinely prospective, policy-regulating relief that can be granted without negating the outstanding judgment. Expanding Heck beyond that necessity test would amount to an extra-textual narrowing of § 1983 that risks insulating ongoing constitutional violations from meaningful judicial review where habeas offers no comparable prospective remedy.

John Roberts.reasoning: Heck’s favorable-termination bar is best applied as an administrable, bright-line limitation on § 1983 suits that function as collateral attacks on an outstanding conviction—most clearly damages actions whose success would establish the conviction’s invalidity. Here, Olivier seeks forward-looking declaratory and injunctive relief against the City’s alleged enforcement practices, and under this Court’s post-Heck cases such prospective challenges are cognizable under § 1983 so long as success would not necessarily negate the validity of the prior judgment. Treating all prospective relief as Heck-barred whenever a plaintiff has any outstanding conviction would expand Heck beyond its finality rationale, invite collateral litigation over the scope of “implies invalidity,” and risk insulating ongoing enforcement regimes from review even where the plaintiff seeks only to prevent future violations. On this record, the proper course is to allow the prospective claims to proceed to the extent they target future enforcement and do not require a judgment that the prior conviction is invalid.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Heck, a §1983 action—regardless of the relief sought—may not proceed if success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment, because that would invite the very “two conflicting resolutions” and federal–state friction Heck sought to prevent. On these facts, Olivier’s requested declaratory and injunctive relief against Brandon’s enforcement practices would require a federal court to adjudge unconstitutional the enforcement that produced his still-valid conviction, thereby necessarily calling that conviction into question. Construing §1983 in light of settled 1871 common-law principles and historically grounded defenses, this favorable-termination rule functions as a limit on collateral civil attacks that would re-litigate issues intertwined with the criminal judgment. Because Olivier has not obtained favorable termination through direct review, state postconviction, or habeas, Heck bars the suit at this time.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Heck bars a § 1983 action when success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, and Olivier’s requested declaratory and injunctive relief—aimed at the City’s enforcement practices underlying his conviction—would functionally require a federal court to pronounce that enforcement unconstitutional in a manner that calls his still-valid conviction into question. Parsing the elements of his theory, he is not merely challenging a general policy in the abstract; he seeks a judicial declaration that the very enforcement that produced his conviction was unlawful, which is an impermissible “attack” unless and until he secures favorable termination through the criminal process or habeas. Wilkinson and Skinner leave room for prospective relief when it would not necessarily undermine the conviction, but this case (as framed) cannot be granted without negating the legal basis for the conviction itself. Consistent with Wallace’s interaction principles, the proper course is to require him to pursue available channels to invalidate the conviction first, rather than using § 1983 to obtain forward-looking relief that effectively operates as collateral review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Heck is an implicit, purpose-limited exception to § 1983 designed to prevent civil suits from functioning as de facto habeas challenges that would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding conviction or sentence. On these facts, Olivier seeks forward-looking declaratory and injunctive relief aimed at restraining the City’s allegedly unconstitutional enforcement practices going forward, not relief that would terminate custody, shorten its duration, or otherwise operate as a direct collateral attack on his conviction in the Preiser sense. Because success would at most regulate future enforcement and does not necessarily negate the legal validity of the prior judgment (as opposed to declaring ongoing practices unconstitutional), extending Heck to bar this suit would overread the doctrine, insulate municipal policies from review, and risk precluding potentially meritorious First Amendment claims without serving Heck’s anti-“swamping” function. The proper course is to allow the prospective claims to proceed (with ordinary doctrines like issue preclusion, standing, and equitable limits doing any necessary case-specific work) rather than impose a categorical favorable-termination bar.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1983 carries an “implicit exception” for claims within the core of habeas, which our Preiser/Heck line-polices by asking whether success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction or sentence—most clearly when the plaintiff seeks “immediate or speedier release.” Here Olivier seeks forward-looking declaratory and injunctive relief aimed at the City’s future enforcement practices, not an order undoing his conviction or shortening his punishment, so the suit is not functionally a collateral attack in habeas’s domain. To be sure, some forms of declaratory relief can collide with Heck if they amount to a ruling that the conviction itself is unlawful; but a properly framed prospective injunction against future enforcement (and an accompanying declaration about the policy’s unconstitutionality going forward) can be adjudicated without granting relief that negates the existing judgment. Reading Heck to categorically bar all prospective challenges by anyone with an outstanding conviction would stretch the doctrine beyond its harmonizing purpose and risk letting § 1983’s remedial scheme be displaced even where habeas cannot supply the forward-looking relief sought.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: We start with Heck’s own limiting principle: a § 1983 action is barred only when success “would necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding conviction. On this record, Olivier seeks forward-looking declaratory and injunctive relief aimed at preventing future enforcement of the City’s practices; that kind of prospective relief does not inevitably negate the validity of the particular past conviction in the way a damages award for unconstitutional conviction would. Our cases draw that line: when the plaintiff’s requested remedy would at most entitle him to constitutionally compliant procedures or constrain future enforcement, § 1983 remains available and Heck does not supply an extra-textual immunity for municipalities. Whether any narrower preclusion or vehicle problems remain is for the lower courts to assess in the first instance under the correct Heck framework on remand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Heck’s favorable-termination principle is a gatekeeper for § 1983 claims that function as collateral attacks on an existing conviction—particularly damages claims that, if successful, would necessarily imply the conviction’s invalidity and thereby create inconsistent civil/criminal judgments. Here, Olivier seeks forward-looking declaratory and injunctive relief against the City’s allegedly unconstitutional enforcement practices, relief that (properly framed) regulates future conduct and does not by itself undo or award damages for the past conviction. Consistent with the functional purposes of favorable-termination (avoiding parallel litigation over guilt/probable cause, preventing inconsistent judgments, and blocking collateral attacks), Heck should not be extended to categorically bar prospective relief simply because the plaintiff has an outstanding conviction; any remaining concerns can be handled by tailoring the remedy and ordinary preclusion/justiciability limits on remand. The administrable rule is that Heck bars § 1983 only when the plaintiff’s claim or requested relief would necessarily invalidate the conviction; prospective injunctions against future enforcement ordinarily do not.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The first question is vehicle: taking state law and the existing conviction as we find them, Olivier’s requested declaratory and injunctive relief is not merely forward-looking in effect if it would require a federal court to hold that the City’s enforcement against him was unconstitutional in a way that would practically obstruct the State’s ability to maintain and enforce his still-outstanding conviction. Under Heck’s intersection-of-remedies logic and the habeas/§ 1983 line, when the relief sought would necessarily imply the invalidity of that conviction (or function as an end-run around the more federalism-protective habeas track), the favorable-termination requirement applies. Olivier can pursue genuinely prospective relief that does not negate his conviction, but on these facts the suit—as framed—invites a determination incompatible with the continued validity of the conviction and thus belongs in habeas or after favorable termination. That boundary-policing prevents § 1983 from becoming a collateral-attack vehicle and respects the procedural choices Congress and this Court have attached to challenges that would undo a criminal judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Heck is a judicially crafted limitation on § 1983 that must be kept tethered to its text and to the habeas–§ 1983 boundary it was designed to police; nothing in § 1983 itself creates a categorical bar on forward-looking declaratory or injunctive relief whenever a plaintiff has an outstanding conviction. Applying Heck’s own standard, Olivier’s suit—aimed at enjoining allegedly unconstitutional municipal enforcement practices going forward—does not "necessarily imply" the invalidity of his past conviction in the way a damages action for wrongful conviction would, because a court could order prospective relief without vacating or otherwise undoing the judgment already entered. Extending Heck to foreclose such prospective challenges would function as an extra-textual narrowing of § 1983 and risk insulating ongoing First and Fourteenth Amendment violations from meaningful judicial review, a result this Court has cautioned against in the § 1983/habeas line. The proper course is to allow the prospective-relief claims to proceed (leaving other doctrines like preclusion, forfeiture, or standing for the lower courts to address in the first instance), rather than expanding Heck beyond its doctrinal justification.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Heck v. Humphrey favorable-termination bar prevents a plaintiff convicted of (or whose criminal judgment remains valid for) resisting/obstruction-type offenses from bringing a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 action seeking prospective injunctive or declaratory relief (and/or damages) challenging the constitutionality of the police actions and municipal policies connected to his arrest.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (as limited by the doctrine of Heck v. Humphrey) and, in substance, the First and Fourth Amendments (speech/assembly and seizure/arrest), with requested equitable relief implicating Article III standing and traditional limits on federal injunctive power.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Olivier argues that Heck should not be read to categorically block § 1983 claims—particularly forward-looking declaratory and injunctive relief—where the plaintiff is not asking the federal court to invalidate his conviction and where success would not necessarily imply the invalidity of the criminal judgment; he contends the Fifth Circuit applied Heck too broadly in a way that insulates allegedly unconstitutional policing and municipal policies from meaningful federal review, including in protest/free-speech contexts.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City of Brandon argues that Olivier’s § 1983 theory (even framed as prospective relief) would, if successful, necessarily call into question the lawfulness of the arrest and related factual/legal predicates underlying his still-valid criminal disposition, triggering Heck’s favorable-termination requirement; respondents further contend the case is a poor vehicle because of threshold problems independent of Heck—such as forfeiture/presentment defects and potential preclusion doctrines (estoppel/res judicata)—and point to related Fifth Circuit litigation (including Siders v. City of Brandon) that may affect or foreclose the claims.
key_precedents: Siders v. City of Brandon, Mississippi

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan is right that Heck is not categorical and that, under Wilkinson, some forward-looking relief may proceed when it can be granted without negating an outstanding conviction. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Alito emphasize, the pleadings here tether the requested declaration and injunction to the asserted unlawfulness of the arrest/enforcement episode that supplied the factual predicates for Olivier’s still-valid resisting/obstruction judgment; granting that relief would, in practical and legal effect, necessarily imply the invalidity of that judgment. The better course is a narrow affirmance grounded in Heck’s “necessarily imply” test as applied to this complaint and this remedial request, while reserving that a genuinely severable, ordinance-focused prospective challenge could present a different case. Article III and equitable-tailoring tools do not eliminate the threshold collateral-attack problem when the relief sought would functionally adjudicate the conviction’s predicates unlawful.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan is right to insist Heck turns on logical necessity, not labels, and Wilkinson leaves room for genuinely prospective relief. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the relief actually pleaded here is keyed to the asserted unlawfulness of the very arrest/enforcement episode that produced a still-valid resisting/obstruction judgment; a declaration or injunction granting that theory would necessarily adjudicate the absence of lawful basis and thus “necessarily imply” invalidity. Read against the closest 1871 common-law analogues (false imprisonment/malicious arrest/malicious prosecution), Olivier’s claim imports want of probable cause and, insofar as it functions like malicious prosecution, favorable termination—requirements he cannot satisfy while the conviction stands. If a future plaintiff pleads a severable, forward-looking decree untethered to the prior conviction, that case may differ, but this complaint is a collateral attack barred by Heck as framed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is that Heck turns on logical necessity and that, under Wilkinson, some prospective relief can be crafted without negating an outstanding conviction. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, this complaint is not a detached, generally applicable challenge; it asks a federal court to declare unconstitutional the very arrest/enforcement episode and municipal practices that supplied the factual predicates for Olivier’s still-valid resisting/obstruction judgment. Even if framed as “prospective,” success here would, in practical and legal effect, necessarily imply that the conviction rests on unconstitutional enforcement—precisely the collateral attack Heck is designed to prevent. I would therefore affirm on the pleadings while leaving open, as Justice Barrett suggests, that a genuinely severable ordinance-focused injunction in a different case might not be barred.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett press the case-specific point that Olivier’s requested declaration/injunction is pleaded around the asserted unlawfulness of the very arrest that preceded his resisting/obstruction conviction, and that granting it would in effect brand the conviction’s predicates unlawful. But Heck is a habeas-channeling, judge-made “implicit exception” to § 1983, and under Wilkinson the bar turns on logical necessity—whether success would necessarily negate an element of the outstanding judgment—not on factual overlap or the practical discomfort of parallel adjudications. If aspects of the prayer would function as a collateral attack, the appropriate response is ordinary remedial tailoring (narrowing or denying particular declaratory language) and, as Justice Gorsuch notes, standing/sequencing limits on what forward-looking relief is available, rather than expanding Heck into a categorical prohibition on prospective challenges to ongoing municipal practices. Because respondents’ rule would convert favorable termination into a broad shield against equitable § 1983 review absent clear congressional direction, I remain for petitioner and would remand for claim-by-claim application of the “necessarily imply” test and equitable limits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett press the strongest point: that the complaint’s requested declaration/injunction, as drafted, appears to hinge on declaring Olivier’s arrest unlawful and so would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of his still-valid resisting/obstruction conviction. But Heck’s favorable-termination rule is a narrow, functional boundary keyed to logical necessity, not a categorical shield whenever a conviction exists; Wilkinson confirms that forward-looking relief may proceed when it can be fashioned without negating the conviction. The proper move, in my view, is not to extend Heck to foreclose all prospective challenges, but to remand so lower courts can apply ordinary equitable tailoring (and, as Justice Gorsuch notes, standing and redressability limits) to excise or deny any conviction-invalidating declaratory language while permitting any genuinely severable prospective relief. Justice Thomas’s common-law-analogy point is relevant for damages claims sounding in false imprisonment/malicious prosecution, but it does not justify converting Heck into a broad bar against municipal-practice injunctions that can be framed without undermining the judgment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan is correct that Heck asks about logical necessity, not thematic overlap, and Wilkinson contemplates prospective relief that can be awarded without casting doubt on an outstanding judgment. But the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett rightly stress that we must analyze this case as pleaded and in the proper sequence: Olivier’s requested declaration and injunction are keyed to the asserted unlawfulness of the very arrest-and-enforcement episode that furnished the factual predicates for his still-valid resisting/obstruction conviction. Granting that relief would, in practical and legal effect, necessarily imply the invalidity of that judgment—the collateral attack Heck forbids absent favorable termination—so this is not the occasion to announce broader rules about severable, ordinance-focused prospective decrees. Standing and equitable tailoring may matter in other cases, but here Heck supplies the limiting principle on these pleadings.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Heck is functional and that, under Wilkinson, some genuinely prospective relief can proceed when it does not necessarily imply invalidity of an outstanding conviction. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Olivier’s pleadings are keyed to the asserted unlawfulness of the very arrest/enforcement episode that supplied the predicates for his still-valid resisting/obstruction judgment; granting the requested declaration and injunction would, in substance, adjudicate the absence of lawful basis and thereby necessarily imply the conviction’s invalidity. That is exactly the gatekeeping role the favorable-termination requirement serves in the Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution analogue—preventing § 1983 from becoming a collateral attack and avoiding parallel relitigation of probable cause and guilt—concerns rooted in Heck’s finality logic. I agree we can leave open that a narrower, truly untethered forward-looking decree might be different, but on these pleadings Heck bars relief absent favorable termination.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan is right that Heck is functional, not categorical, and that Wilkinson leaves room for genuinely prospective relief that can be awarded without negating an outstanding conviction. But the Chief Justice’s point remains dispositive here: as pleaded, Olivier’s requested declaration and injunction are keyed to the asserted unlawfulness of the very arrest-and-enforcement episode that produced his still-valid resisting/obstruction judgment, so success would necessarily imply its invalidity in substance even if styled as “forward-looking.” I would resist Justice Gorsuch’s impulse to recast that defect as Article III standing, because that would improperly transform a merits limitation on § 1983’s availability into a constitutional jurisdictional rule beyond Congress’s domain. A narrow affirmance can make clear that a severable, ordinance-focused prospective challenge might present a different case, but these pleadings do not.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett fairly identify a remedial overbreadth problem: certain forms of declaratory language about the lawfulness of Olivier’s arrest could, if granted, "necessarily imply" the invalidity of the resisting/obstruction conviction. But that point goes to tailoring and partial dismissal, not to converting Heck into a categorical bar on forward-looking § 1983 relief whenever an outstanding conviction exists; Wilkinson confirms that prospective relief may proceed when it can be fashioned without negating the judgment. As Justice Kagan notes, Heck’s inquiry is one of logical necessity, and ordinary tools—equitable discretion, preclusion principles, and careful remedial framing—can prevent collateral attack without insulating ongoing municipal practices from § 1983 scrutiny absent a clear congressional command. I would remand for that doctrine-bound sorting rather than affirming a broad foreclosure rule tied to the pleadings’ current phrasing.

John Roberts.reasoning: The threshold question is whether Olivier’s § 1983 claims—though styled as prospective declaratory and injunctive relief—would in substance “necessarily imply” the invalidity of the still-valid resisting/obstruction-type disposition arising from the same arrest, and on this record his theory appears to do exactly that by attacking the lawfulness of the officers’ conduct and the municipal policies that formed the predicate for the conviction. Heck’s bar is not limited to damages labels; where the requested declaration would function as an adjudication that the arrest and ensuing prosecution lacked lawful basis, it collides with the finality interests Heck protects and becomes an impermissible collateral attack absent favorable termination. Nothing presented shows a narrow, forward-looking injunction targeted only at future enforcement and decoupled from the factual and legal predicates of his past judgment in the way Wilkinson permits; instead, the equitable relief is intertwined with, and would effectively negate, the validity of the existing criminal judgment. Given those threshold constraints—and the vehicle concerns respondents identify—Heck precludes the action as brought.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Starting with § 1983’s text, it contains no favorable-termination requirement, so any such bar must be justified—if at all—by a historically grounded, closest-analogue inquiry. Olivier’s claims arise from police conduct culminating in an arrest and a still-valid conviction for resisting/obstruction-type offenses; the closest 1871 tort analogues for such arrest-based claims (false imprisonment/malicious arrest and, to the extent he challenges process leading to conviction, malicious prosecution) traditionally required want of probable cause and, for prosecution-type claims, favorable termination—elements that his theory would necessarily negate if he obtained a declaration/injunction that the arrest and its predicates were unconstitutional. Because the prospective relief he seeks is not meaningfully severable from the lawfulness of the arrest and the factual predicates supporting the resisting/obstruction judgment, success would “necessarily imply” invalidity in the sense relevant to Heck, so the action cannot proceed while the conviction remains outstanding. Whatever the proper historical limits of Heck in other contexts, this case falls on the arrest/conviction side of the line and thus is barred absent favorable termination.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Heck v. Humphrey, a § 1983 action is barred when success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment, and that principle cannot be evaded by relabeling the requested remedy as declaratory or injunctive relief. On these facts, Olivier’s proposed declaration and injunction would rest on the premise that the officers’ conduct and the City’s policies made the arrest unlawful, which would directly call into question elements and factual predicates of his still-valid resisting/obstruction-type conviction. Extending § 1983 equitable relief in this posture would undermine finality and invite collateral federal review of state criminal judgments—practical consequences Heck was designed to prevent—especially where alternative avenues (direct review, habeas, state processes) exist for attacking the conviction itself. Whatever room Wilkinson v. Dotson leaves for prospective relief, it does not cover claims that, as here, necessarily negate the lawfulness of the underlying arrest tied to an unvacated conviction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Preiser, habeas is exclusive only for claims that functionally seek to alter the fact or duration of custody; Olivier’s suit, as framed, seeks prospective declaratory and injunctive relief against future enforcement of an ordinance and related municipal policies, not release, shorter custody, or vacatur of his past conviction. Applying Heck’s “necessarily imply the invalidity” test narrowly—as an implicit, judge-made limitation designed to prevent § 1983 from displacing habeas—success on Olivier’s forward-looking First Amendment challenge would not necessarily negate every element of his prior resisting/obstruction-type disposition, particularly where the requested relief can be granted without adjudicating that the prior judgment is invalid. Extending Heck to categorically bar prospective relief here would go beyond Heck’s structural rationale and improperly insulate allegedly unconstitutional policing and protest restrictions from the “broad spectrum” of judicial review Congress authorized in § 1983. Any remaining concerns about issue preclusion, standing, or tailoring equitable relief are better addressed through those doctrines rather than by an overbroad favorable-termination bar.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The first question is where Olivier’s suit sits on the § 1983–habeas boundary: under Preiser and Wilkinson, § 1983 has an “implicit exception” only for claims whose success would place them within the core of habeas—i.e., those that would necessarily undermine the fact or duration of confinement or otherwise invalidate an extant judgment. On these facts, a forward-looking request to enjoin or declare unconstitutional the City’s arrest/protest-enforcement policies (and any future enforcement of the challenged ordinance/practices) does not, by its own operation, negate Olivier’s still-valid resisting/obstruction disposition; it regulates future conduct and can succeed without a finding that his conviction is invalid. Heck therefore bars only those aspects of Olivier’s theory (particularly damages or declaratory relief keyed to the unlawfulness of his specific arrest) that would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of elements essential to his conviction, but it does not categorically foreclose prospective equitable relief that can be granted consistent with the existing judgment. The Fifth Circuit’s rule treating injunctions as Heck-barred simply because the plaintiff was previously convicted sweeps beyond Heck’s functional test and risks converting the “implicit exception” into a broad immunity for ongoing municipal policies.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Our cases require courts to proceed in the right order: before reaching Heck’s merits bar, a plaintiff seeking prospective declaratory or injunctive relief must establish Article III standing by showing a real and immediate threat of future injury, and on this record Olivier’s requested forward-looking relief appears tethered to a past arrest and completed prosecution rather than a concrete, imminent risk of repetition. Even setting standing aside, Heck turns on whether success would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an existing criminal judgment, and a § 1983 theory attacking the constitutionality of the arrest and the municipal policies that produced it would, as pleaded here, tend to negate predicates commonly essential to resisting/obstruction-type convictions—making this suit an impermissible collateral attack absent favorable termination. Wilkinson v. Dotson preserves room for truly prospective challenges that do not undermine a conviction, but it does not authorize federal courts to issue declaratory or injunctive relief whose logic would effectively brand the still-valid conviction unlawful. Applying Heck’s limiting principle as written, I would affirm the Fifth Circuit’s judgment in favor of the City.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Heck v. Humphrey, a § 1983 plaintiff cannot maintain a claim—whether styled as damages or declaratory/injunctive relief—if success would necessarily imply the invalidity of a still-valid criminal judgment. Here, Olivier’s prosecution for resisting/obstruction-type offenses remains valid, and his requested relief (a declaration and injunction premised on the alleged unconstitutionality of the arresting officers’ actions and related municipal policies) would functionally relitigate the lawfulness of the arrest and the predicates for his conviction, creating exactly the parallel civil/criminal litigation and inconsistency concerns Heck was designed to prevent. Applying the common-law malicious-prosecution analogue as the organizing framework, favorable termination is a threshold element; Olivier cannot satisfy it because the prosecution did not end without a conviction. Absent that threshold showing, the federal courts should not allow § 1983 to operate as a collateral attack on the outstanding conviction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The key constraint here is not Article III standing but Heck’s merits-based limit on the availability of a § 1983 cause of action while an outstanding criminal judgment remains valid; we should not “transform” that merits inquiry into a jurisdictional defect. On these facts, Olivier’s requested declaratory/injunctive relief and damages—aimed at declaring unconstitutional the arrest and related municipal policies connected to the very incident that produced his still-valid resisting/obstruction-type conviction—would, if granted, necessarily undermine the lawfulness of predicates the criminal judgment depends on, triggering Heck’s favorable-termination rule “no matter the relief sought.” Because success in the § 1983 suit would functionally call into question the validity of the extant conviction, federal adjudication now would amount to an impermissible collateral attack rather than outcome-neutral prospective relief. Absent a vacatur or other favorable termination, Heck bars the action on the merits, so I would affirm for the City.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting with § 1983’s text and this Court’s precedent, Heck is a narrow, historically grounded limitation that bars only those § 1983 claims whose success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment, and it should not be expanded atextually to foreclose forward-looking relief. On these facts—where Olivier seeks prospective declaratory/injunctive relief targeting police practices and municipal policies connected to protest policing—the question is whether a federal judgment would necessarily negate an essential element of his still-valid resisting/obstruction-type conviction; absent that tight logical link, Heck does not apply. Extending Heck to categorically bar prospective challenges would insulate allegedly unconstitutional policing from meaningful judicial review and raise constitutional-backdrop concerns by forcing citizens to risk (or endure) prosecution with no effective federal forum to prevent future liberty-depriving violations. The proper course is to permit the § 1983 suit to proceed to the ordinary Article III and equitable-relief inquiries (standing, threat of future injury, scope of injunction), rather than using Heck as an overbroad gatekeeping rule.
